items.prompt: State what is meant by the rapid increase in the world's population.
items.canonical_answer: The steep rise in the total number of people on Earth that began around 1750, from about 1 billion in 1800 to about 8 billion in 2022.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the meaning - a steep, accelerating rise in the total, with a period or a figure that dates it. "More people" alone is not the term.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 1.1 claim ledger.
objective_titles: Describe and give reasons for the rapid increase in the world’s population

items.prompt: Explain why the world's population began to increase rapidly from around 1750.
items.canonical_answer: Cleaner water, better sanitation, vaccines and more reliable food supplies cut the death rate, because far fewer people died from disease and hunger. Birth rates stayed high for a time, so births greatly outnumbered deaths. Because the gap between the two rates stayed wide for decades, the population grew steeply.
marking_guidance: 1 mark each, to 3: a named cause of falling deaths (medicine, sanitation, food); which causes the death rate to fall; so births exceed deaths and the population grows.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 1.1 claim ledger.
objective_titles: Describe and give reasons for the rapid increase in the world’s population

items.prompt:
A class plots the world's population, in billions, at six dates:

| year | 1750 | 1850 | 1950 | 2000 | 2011 | 2022 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| population / billions | 0.8 | 1.3 | 2.5 | 6.1 | 7.0 | 8.0 |

Describe how the world's population changed over this period.
items.canonical_answer: The table shows the population rising slowly at first and then steeply. It grew by only 0.5 billion in the century after 1750, from 0.8 to 1.3 billion, but by 1.2 billion between 1850 and 1950, and by 3.6 billion between 1950 and 2000. From 2000 to 2022 it rose by 1.9 billion, so the increase per year is far larger now than in the eighteenth century.
marking_guidance: Reading: the pattern read from the table - a slow rise at first and a steep rise later (1 mark).

Values: the figures for at least two periods, with their units in billions, which show the growth accelerating (1 mark); the contrast between the earliest and latest growth rates made explicit, so the figures support the words (1 mark).
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 1.1 claim ledger.
objective_titles: Describe and give reasons for the rapid increase in the world’s population

items.prompt: A country introduced a vaccination programme and clean piped water to its towns in the 1980s. Its birth rate in 1990 was 44 per 1000 and its death rate was 14 per 1000; in 1970 both had been 44 per 1000 and 22 per 1000. Suggest why its population began to grow rapidly in the 1980s.
items.canonical_answer: The vaccination programme and clean water cut deaths from disease, which suggests why the death rate fell from 22 to 14 per 1000. The birth rate stayed high at 44 per 1000, so the resource given here shows births far outnumbering deaths. Because the gap between the two rates widened to 30 per 1000, the population grew rapidly.
marking_guidance: Resource: the evidence used - the death rate falls (14 per 1000) while the birth rate stays high (44 per 1000), because the health measures explain the fall in deaths (1 mark).
Reasons: the wider gap between births and deaths means faster growth (1 mark); the arithmetic of the gap, so the reason is carried by the resource's figures (1 mark).
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 1.1 claim ledger.
objective_titles: Describe and give reasons for the rapid increase in the world’s population

items.prompt: Asked to explain why the population of Germany, a wealthy country, is falling, a learner writes: "Because of famine, and poor sanitation in the cities." Explain the error.
items.canonical_answer: The learner has used causes of high death rates in low-income countries, famine and poor sanitation, which is the wrong angle for a wealthy country. In Germany deaths outnumber births because the birth rate is low and the population is ageing, so the fall comes from the birth rate, not from disease or hunger. The test is which countries the resource shows and what drives change there: in a wealthier country, the demographic cause, not the health one.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the confusion named - famine and poor sanitation are causes of high death rates, wrongly used for a wealthy country's falling population.
1 mark: the correct idea - a low birth rate and an ageing population, so deaths exceed births.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 1.1 claim ledger.
objective_titles: Describe and give reasons for the rapid increase in the world’s population

items.prompt: A learner writes: "China is over-populated because it has more than 1400 million people." Explain the error.
items.canonical_answer: A large number of people is not what over-population means, so the answer is not about people compared with resources. Over-population is too many people for the resources and technology of an area to support a good standard of living. Whether China is over-populated depends on whether its farms, water, housing and jobs can support its people well, not on the count.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the error named - treating over-population as "a lot of people", which is not the same as the defined term.
1 mark: the correct idea - the judgement compares people with the resources and technology of the area.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 1.1 claim ledger.
objective_titles: Describe and give reasons for the rapid increase in the world’s population

items.prompt: State what is meant by over-population.
items.canonical_answer: Too many people for the resources and technology of an area to support a good standard of living.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the meaning - people relative to resources and technology; "a large population" alone is not the term.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 1.1 claim ledger.
objective_titles: Show an understanding of over-population and under-population

items.prompt: Explain how an area becomes over-populated.
items.canonical_answer: An area becomes over-populated when its people multiply past what its resources and technology can support. The land cannot feed everyone, so food is short, and housing, schools and hospitals become overloaded because services were built for fewer people. Over-population therefore causes a falling standard of living, because the same resources must be shared among more and more people.
marking_guidance: 1 mark each, to 3: more people than the resources or technology support; which causes hunger or overloaded services; so the standard of living falls.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 1.1 claim ledger.
objective_titles: Show an understanding of over-population and under-population

items.prompt: State the two main causes of a change in the size of a country's population.
items.canonical_answer: Natural change, the balance of births and deaths, and migration, the balance of people entering and leaving the country.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the meaning - both natural change (births and deaths) and migration named as the two causes.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 1.1 claim ledger.
objective_titles: Understand the main causes of a change in population size

items.prompt: Explain why the birth rate is high in many low-income countries.
items.canonical_answer: Where many children die young, parents have large families so that some survive, which keeps the birth rate high. Children also work on the family holding, so a large family is a benefit there. Because few women are in paid work or education, marriage and childbearing start early, so a woman has children across more of her life.
marking_guidance: 1 mark each, to 3: high child mortality leads to large families; children as workers on the family holding; so early marriage and little schooling for women keep births numerous.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 1.1 claim ledger.
objective_titles: Understand the main causes of a change in population size

items.prompt:
The table shows the number of deaths, in thousands, in two countries in 2020:

| cause | disease linked to dirty water | malaria | famine-related | road accidents | other |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| country A | 210 | 95 | 60 | 30 | 205 |
| country B | 3 | 1 | 0 | 35 | 261 |

Describe the differences between the two countries' deaths.
items.canonical_answer: The table shows country A losing far more people to causes that wealth prevents: 210 000 deaths from water-borne disease and 95 000 from malaria, against 3000 and 1000 in country B. Country B's deaths are concentrated in "other" causes, 261 000, which is more than country A's 205 000, so its people die of other things at older ages rather than of hunger and dirty water. Country A's famine-related 60 000 deaths have no counterpart at all in country B.
marking_guidance: Reading: the pattern read from the table - country A's deaths are dominated by poverty-related causes, country B's are not (1 mark).

Values: the contrasting figures with units, 210 000 against 3000 for water-borne disease (1 mark); a second paired reading, such as the famine-related 60 000 against 0, which the figures support (1 mark).

objective_titles: Understand the main causes of a change in population size

items.prompt: A survey of a rural district finds that most families have five or more children, that few girls attend secondary school, and that most people farm small plots. Suggest why the district's population is growing quickly.
items.canonical_answer: The resource suggests children are needed as workers on the small plots, because most people farm and each pair of hands matters. Few girls in secondary school suggests women marry and begin childbearing early, so births are spread across more of a woman's life. Because families want and have five or more children, the birth rate far exceeds the death rate, which means the district's population grows quickly.
marking_guidance: Resource: the evidence used - farming families need many hands, so large families are an advantage here (1 mark).
Reasons: little schooling for girls means early marriage and childbearing, so births are numerous (1 mark); therefore births exceed deaths and the population grows quickly (1 mark).
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 1.1 claim ledger.
objective_titles: Understand the main causes of a change in population size

items.prompt: Give the definition of the term birth rate.
items.canonical_answer: The number of live births per 1000 people in a year.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the meaning - live births per 1000 people per year; the per-1000 basis is part of the term.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 1.1 claim ledger.
objective_titles: Give reasons for contrasting rates of natural population change

items.prompt: Explain why the rate of natural population change differs between a low-income country and a high-income country.
items.canonical_answer: In many low-income countries vaccination and clean water have cut the death rate, while the birth rate has stayed high, because children still work on farms and women have little schooling. The result is a wide gap between births and deaths. In high-income countries both rates are low: family planning is normal and the population is older, so deaths roughly match or exceed births, which means natural change is small or negative.
marking_guidance: 1 mark each, to 3: in the low-income country deaths fall first while births stay high; because of the causes on each side (farming families, little schooling; family planning, ageing); so the gap between the two countries' natural change follows from the timing of the two falls.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 1.1 claim ledger.
objective_titles: Give reasons for contrasting rates of natural population change

items.prompt:
The table gives rates for four countries in the early 2020s:

| country | birth rate / per 1000 | death rate / per 1000 |
|---|---|---|
| Niger | 45 | 9 |
| Bangladesh | 18 | 9 |
| United Kingdom | 11 | 9 |
| Japan | 7 | 12 |

Describe the contrasts in natural population change between these countries.
items.canonical_answer: The table shows natural change falling steadily down the list. Niger's births exceed its deaths by 36 per 1000, so its population grows by about 3.6 per cent a year. Bangladesh grows by 9 per 1000 and the United Kingdom by 2 per 1000, both on the same death rate of 9. Japan is the outlier: its deaths (12 per 1000) outnumber its births (7 per 1000), so its population shrinks by 5 per 1000 each year.
marking_guidance: Reading: the pattern read from the table - natural change (births minus deaths) falls from country to country and turns negative (1 mark).

Values: at least two differences worked from the figures with units, such as Niger's 36 per 1000 and Japan's -5 per 1000 (1 mark); the outlier or the shared death rate noted, so the figures support the words (1 mark).
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 1.1 claim ledger.
objective_titles: Give reasons for contrasting rates of natural population change

items.prompt: A country's health ministry reports: "Deaths have fallen sharply now that most children receive their vaccinations. Every child still helps on the family farm, and there are no family planning clinics outside the capital." Suggest what will happen to this country's natural population change.
items.canonical_answer: The statement suggests the death rate has fallen sharply, because vaccinated children survive. The birth rate will stay high, because children still work the farms and family planning is absent outside the capital. So natural increase, births minus deaths, will grow wider, which means the population grows faster than before.
marking_guidance: Resource: the evidence used - the vaccination programme cuts deaths, and no clinics and farm labour keep births high (1 mark).
Reasons: the fall in deaths arrives before any fall in births (1 mark); therefore the natural increase widens and growth accelerates (1 mark).
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 1.1 claim ledger.
objective_titles: Give reasons for contrasting rates of natural population change

items.prompt: A learner writes: "The country grew by 50 000 people last year, so its natural increase was 50 000." Explain what is confused here.
items.canonical_answer: Total population change and natural increase are not the same. The 50 000 is the whole change, which adds natural increase, births minus deaths, to net migration, immigrants minus emigrants. If 5000 more people entered than left, natural increase would be 45 000. The test is whether the change is caused by births and deaths, or by people moving in and out.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the confusion named - total change is not the same as natural increase, because migration is part of the total.
1 mark: the correct idea - natural increase is births minus deaths; net migration is immigrants minus emigrants; the two add to the total.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 1.1 claim ledger.
objective_titles: Give reasons for contrasting rates of natural population change

items.prompt: A learner calculates natural increase for a birth rate of 32 per 1000 and a death rate of 8 per 1000 by dividing: "32 ÷ 8 = 4 per 1000." Explain the error.
items.canonical_answer: Natural increase is a difference, not a division: 32 - 8 = 24 per 1000. The learner has divided the two rates instead of subtracting them, which gives a number with no meaning. The test is whether the answer is a difference, in per 1000.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the error named - the rates are divided instead of subtracted, which is the wrong operation.
1 mark: the correct calculation - 32 - 8 = 24 per 1000, a difference in per 1000 per year.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 1.1 claim ledger.
objective_titles: Give reasons for contrasting rates of natural population change

items.prompt: Describe two benefits of an anti-natalist policy that provides family planning and keeps girls in school.
items.canonical_answer: Family planning services let couples choose when and whether to have children, which means the birth rate falls and each family can spend more on each child. Educated girls marry and begin childbearing later, which benefits the country with a smaller, better-fed school-age cohort and, later, more women able to earn.
marking_guidance: 1 mark per benefit, 2 in all: chosen childbearing means a falling birth rate; educated girls marry later, which means fewer births and better-supported children.
Each benefit is taken to its consequence, because or so or which means.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 1.1 claim ledger.
objective_titles: Describe and evaluate population policies

items.prompt: Describe two problems a strict anti-natalist policy can cause later on.
items.canonical_answer: A sharp fall in births shrinks the future workforce, which means there are fewer workers to support each older person. The policy can also change the balance of the sexes, because where families prefer a son, a one-child limit leads to sex-selective births, which means millions of men cannot find partners, as happened in China by the 2010s.
marking_guidance: 1 mark per problem, 2 in all: a shrinking workforce supports a large older cohort; sex-selective births unbalance the population.
Each problem is taken to its consequence, because or so or which means.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 1.1 claim ledger.
objective_titles: Describe and evaluate population policies

items.prompt: A government claims its strict one-child policy was a complete success. Using what you know about China's policy from 1979 to 2015, suggest how far you would agree.
items.canonical_answer: The judgement is that the policy succeeded in its aim but not without costs. It achieved a sharp fall in the birth rate, which was its purpose, so on its own terms it worked. But a complete success would leave the country healthy as well as smaller, and China's ageing population, its shrinking workforce and its millions of extra men are evidence that the fall in births created problems the policy did not foresee. So the judgement is partly agree: the policy met its goal, and its side-effects were the price.
marking_guidance: Judgement: a stated decision - partly agree, with the extent made clear (1 mark).
Because: the reasoning - the birth rate fell, which was the aim (1 mark); so the side-effects, ageing, workforce, sex balance, are weighed as evidence against "complete" (1 mark).
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 1.1 claim ledger.
objective_titles: Describe and evaluate population policies

items.prompt: Asked "What impacts did the policy have?", a learner lists its measures: clinics, free contraception and school lessons. Explain the error.
items.canonical_answer: The question asks for the results of the policy, but the learner has described how the policy works, which is a different thing. The measures are what the policy does; the impacts are what it achieved, such as a lower birth rate or a smaller school-age cohort. The test is whether the question asks about the measures or the results.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the error named - measures are not the same as impacts, so the answer is the wrong angle for the question.
1 mark: the correct idea - the answer names the policy's results, such as a falling birth rate.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 1.1 claim ledger.
objective_titles: Describe and evaluate population policies

items.prompt:
A carding exercise compares birth rates per 1000 in China:

| year | 1970 | 1980 | 1990 | 2000 | 2010 | 2020 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| birth rate / per 1000 | 33 | 18 | 21 | 14 | 12 | 8 |

Describe what the table shows about China's birth rate over the period of the one-child policy.
items.canonical_answer: The table shows the birth rate falling steeply across the period. It was 33 per 1000 in 1970, before the policy began in 1979, and 18 per 1000 by 1980, so the fall at the start is the sharpest. There is a small rise to 21 per 1000 in 1990, but the trend after that is steadily down, to 8 per 1000 by 2020. The pattern shown is a policy-era fall from around 20 per 1000 to around 10, followed by a further fall after the policy ended.

Values: the figures with units, 33 down to 8 per 1000, read at dated points (1 mark); the exception or the post-policy trend noted, so the figures support the words (1 mark).

items.prompt: For Bangladesh, describe two features that show it is over-populated.
items.canonical_answer: Farms average well under a hectare, and each inheritance divides them further, so the land cannot feed the families on it. Services are overloaded: city schools run several shifts a day and rural clinics serve far more people than they were built for.
marking_guidance: 1 mark per feature, 2 in all: farmland too small per family; overloaded schools or clinics.
Each fact is a feature of the named country, Bangladesh, not a general point about population.

items.prompt: Bangladesh has about 170 million people (2022) on a small delta plain, and its birth rate has fallen from about 34 per 1000 in the 1980s to around 18 by the early 2020s. Explain how this pressure shows in daily life there and what the country has done about it.
items.canonical_answer: The example shows the pressure in work and services: job seekers outnumber formal jobs, which keeps pay low, and schools and clinics serve far more people than they were built for, so standards fall. Because farms are tiny, each family depends on scarce wage work as well as its plot. Bangladesh has responded with family planning, so health workers take contraception to villages and girls' schooling has risen, which means the birth rate has almost halved since the 1980s.
marking_guidance: 1 mark each, to 4, each point using the example: jobs outnumbered by seekers, so pay is low; services over capacity, so quality falls; small farms force families onto wages; the response - village family planning and schooling, so the birth rate fell.
The answer stays with the given example, Bangladesh, and does not generalise to all countries.

objective_titles: A case study of a country which is over-populated

items.prompt: For Australia, describe two features that show it is under-populated.
items.canonical_answer: It has about 26 million people on 7.7 million square kilometres, around 3 per square kilometre, so most people cluster in a few coastal cities while the interior stays nearly empty. Inland farms, mines and services cannot find workers, so resources are wasted and markets are too thin to support services.
marking_guidance: 1 mark per feature, 2 in all: the density figure with the empty interior; resources unworked for lack of labour.
Each fact is a feature of the named country, Australia, not a general point about population.

items.prompt: Australia is rich in minerals and grazing land, yet its interior has too few people to work them. Explain how this under-population came about and how the country responds.
items.canonical_answer: The example shows a desert continent: water, not space, decides where people live, so settlement stopped at the well-watered coast and the interior stayed thin. Because farms and mines inland cannot recruit, resources are wasted and services are too far from their users to survive. Australia responds with a skilled migration scheme, so the country selects the workers the interior and professional services need, which brings in labour that the interior cannot grow itself.
marking_guidance: 1 mark each, to 4, each point using the example: the desert sets the limit, so people cluster on the coast; inland employers cannot recruit, so resources are wasted; the response is skilled migration; which supplies labour the interior cannot grow itself.

items.prompt: For Niger, describe two features of its high rate of natural population growth.
items.canonical_answer: Its birth rate is around 45 per 1000 against a death rate around 9 per 1000, so it grows close to 3.7 per cent a year and doubles in about two decades. Nearly half the population is under 15, so schools and clinics must serve an enormous child cohort.
marking_guidance: 1 mark per feature, 2 in all: the rates and growth pace with units; the young age structure and its pressure on services.
Each fact is a feature of the named country, Niger, not a general point about growth.

items.prompt: In Niger most people farm, girls marry young and average only a few years of school, and children support their parents in old age. Suggest why these features keep the birth rate high.
items.canonical_answer: This example suggests children are the parents' old-age support on family farms, so families have many. Because girls marry young and leave school after a few years, childbearing begins early and lasts long. And because most people farm, every child is a pair of hands, so there is little reason to stop at two.
marking_guidance: Resource: the evidence used - children as support and as farm labour (1 mark).
Reasons: early marriage extends childbearing years (1 mark); so with no reason to limit family size, the birth rate stays high, as it does here (1 mark).

items.prompt: Aid agencies warn that Niger's population will double in about two decades. Suggest whether this growth is best judged as an opportunity or a problem for the country, and justify your judgement.
items.canonical_answer: The judgement is that it is more a problem than an opportunity, because the evidence is against the growth being absorbed. Nearly half the population is already under 15, so the country must school and feed an enormous child cohort on Sahel farm land, and harvests already fail, as they did for millions of people in 2021-22. An opportunity case exists, a young workforce in time, but only if schools and jobs arrive first, and the figures, 3.7 per cent growth a year on failing harvests, suggest they will not arrive fast enough.
marking_guidance: Judgement: a stated decision - more a problem, with the reasoning made clear (1 mark).
Because: the evidence - the child cohort, the failed harvests with figures (1 mark); so the opportunity case is weighed and found weaker, on the growth data given (1 mark).

items.prompt: For Japan, describe two features of its population decline.
items.canonical_answer: Deaths outnumber births, with a death rate near 12-13 per 1000 against a birth rate near 6-7 per 1000, so the population has fallen every year since about 2010 and stood near 124 million in 2023. About 29-30 per cent of the population is 65 or over, so a shrinking workforce supports a very large older cohort.
marking_guidance: 1 mark per feature, 2 in all: deaths exceeding births with the year of peak; the share aged 65 or over with its consequence.
Each fact is a feature of the named country, Japan, not a general point about decline.

items.prompt: In Japan, city housing is expensive, parents pay heavily for children's education, and marriages happen late or not at all. Suggest why these features keep the birth rate near 6-7 per 1000.
items.canonical_answer: This example suggests a child is very expensive in the city, because housing and education both cost heavily, so couples delay. Because marriages happen late or not at all, childbearing starts late and finishes early. And so the one-child family becomes the norm, which means the birth rate stays near 6-7 per 1000 and the population keeps shrinking.
marking_guidance: Resource: the evidence used - the cost of housing and education deters large families (1 mark).
Reasons: late marriage shortens the childbearing years (1 mark); so births stay below deaths and the decline continues, as the figures here show (1 mark).

items.prompt: Japan pays parental leave and child benefits, and lets in some migrant workers, yet its population still falls. Suggest how successful its policy response has been, and justify your judgement.
items.canonical_answer: The judgement is that the response has slowed the decline but not reversed it. The payments and leave give parents support, which is why they remain in place, but the figures - a birth rate near 6-7 per 1000 against deaths near 12-13 - show births still far below deaths, and the intake of migrants is small. The evidence, an ageing population of about 29-30 per cent over 65 and closing rural services, suggests money alone does not change city living costs, so the policy has had limited success.
marking_guidance: Judgement: a stated decision - limited success, slowed but not reversed (1 mark).
Because: the evidence - the rates and the small migrant intake (1 mark); so the reasoning weighs the payments against the living costs that keep births low (1 mark).

items.prompt: For a named country which is over-populated, describe the evidence that shows it is over-populated and assess what its government has done in response. [7]
items.canonical_answer: Bangladesh, a low-income country on the Ganges delta, had about 170 million people in 2022 on a plain smaller than many countries' provinces, with the birth rate around 18 per 1000 and the death rate around 9 per 1000 in the early 2020s. The evidence is in the land: farms average well under a hectare, and each inheritance divides them further, so fields too small to feed a family are worked anyway on the fertile but crowded delta. The evidence is in services too: city schools such as those in Dhaka run several shifts a day, and rural clinics serve far more people than they were built for, while job seekers outnumber formal jobs and pay stays low. The government has pushed back with family planning: health workers take contraception out to the villages, girls' schooling has risen, and the birth rate has come down from about 34 per 1000 in the 1980s to around 18 by the early 2020s. The response has had real effect, but the population, about 170 million and growing around 1 per cent a year, shows the pressure is eased, not ended.
marking_guidance: Level 1 (1-3): simple statements about an over-populated country, with no named example or only general points about crowding.
Level 2 (4-6): developed and linked statements about a named country, capped at 5 if no named example is given.

Level 3 (7): comprehensive statements with place-specific detail - Bangladesh, the Ganges delta, the hectare-sized farms, the shifts-run schools, the birth-rate figures with years - covering both the evidence and the response.

(c) Describe the difference in total population change between the two countries. [3]
(d) Suggest one reason, other than family planning, why country P's birth rate is high. [2]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) Country P.
(b) 36 - 10 = 26 per 1000 per year.
(c) Country P grows by 24 per 1000 overall, 26 of natural increase minus 2 of net migration, so it gains 24 people per 1000 each year. Country Q's natural change is 9 - 11 = -2 per 1000, a natural decrease, but migration of +3 outweighs it, so Q still grows, by 1 per 1000. The table therefore shows P growing far faster than Q, 24 against 1 per 1000, even though P loses people to migration while Q gains them.
(d) Children work on the family holding, so a large family is an advantage where most people farm.

Figures: (c) 3 marks - the natural changes worked with figures (26 and -2 per 1000), the migration balances brought in, and the total changes compared with units.
Marks: (d) 2 marks - one reason for the high birth rate developed with its consequence.
